conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted for right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about your symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this pain before—same spot, under my ribs. It started a few days ago. I had a low-grade fever at home, around 99.6, and felt nauseous. My hepatologist started me on doxycycline, but I wasn’t getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of primary sclerosing cholangitis and past cholangitis episodes, this could be another flare. We’ll run some tests to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried it might be. I’ve had this so many times. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s treatable. We’ll start antibiotics right away to cover any infection, even though you’re not running a high fever now. We also need to check if there’s a stone blocking your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time there was a stone. Can’t they just remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll find out. You’re scheduled for an ultrasound first. If we see a stone, we may need an MRCP or ERCP to get a better look and possibly remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound is back. It shows a retained stone in the central intrahepatic ducts, possibly in the right hepatic duct. No bile duct dilation, which is good, but it could still be causing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s the same stone again? Why can’t they get it out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s in a tricky spot. But we’re not giving up. We’re ordering an MRCP tomorrow for a more detailed view. That’ll help us plan the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the antibiotics? You said you’d start me on something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting IV meropenem. It’s broad-spectrum and safe for you, given your allergies to sulfa and penicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I had diarrhea last time on doxycycline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that. For now, focus on resting. We’ll check your labs and see how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood and urine cultures came back negative—no infection in the blood. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t have an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cultures are negative, but your symptoms and history suggest cholangitis. We’re continuing meropenem because it’s likely a bile duct issue that doesn’t always show up in blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the MRCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for tomorrow morning. It’ll show us the exact location of the stone and the condition of your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRCP is done. It shows a 5 mm filling defect in the common hepatic duct—likely a stone. There’s also confirmation of your PSC changes: fibrosis and irregular ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So they can remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ve scheduled an ERCP for tomorrow. We’ll try to remove the stone using a balloon sweep. Given it’s embedded, we may use a special scope—Spyglass—to see it directly and take biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Biopsies? Is there a cancer concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s precautionary. Sometimes tissue grows over stones, and we want to make sure it’s not abnormal. But your prior tests were negative, so we’re optimistic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will I know how it went?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure is at 12 tomorrow. I’ll come by afterward to update you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the ERCP. The good news: we found an embedded stone in the common hepatic duct. We used Spyglass and biopsies to loosen it, then cleared a portion with a balloon sweep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At least part of it. We got a piece out, and the duct is now draining better. The tissue over the stone showed chronic inflammation, which fits your PSC. The biopsies will be checked for IgG4 to rule out another condition, but that’s routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still improving. We’re switching from IV meropenem to oral ciprofloxacin. You’ll take it for 9 more days at home. After that, resume your rifaximin for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely by Friday. We’ll watch your labs and make sure you’re stable. Your liver enzymes are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are trending well. WBC is normal, bilirubin is down. We’re confident you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel better already. Less pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on cipro, ursodiol, and your other meds. We’re adding a mild laxative, senna, in case the oxycodone for pain causes constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. I’ll drink more water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Fiber too—fruits and veggies. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ at the liver center in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. Your final labs look good. No fever, pain is minimal, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. Will I keep getting these stones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With PSC, there’s a risk, but rifaximin helps reduce flares. We’ll monitor with imaging as needed. The ERCP helped clear the blockage, which should reduce recurrence for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other conditions—thyroid, blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All stable. You’ll continue levothyroxine, lisinopril, furosemide, and omeprazole. No changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And depression? I’ve been feeling down with all these hospital visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re feeling that way. Keep taking your escitalopram. Please mention this at your follow-up—mental health is part of your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Take ciprofloxacin twice daily for 9 days, then restart rifaximin. Use oxycodone only if needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the senna?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if you’re constipated. Drink fluids and eat fiber first. Call if you have fever, worsening pain, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee. Happy Birthday, by the way—I saw it on your badge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oh—thank you! That’s very kind. Take care, and I hope your next visit is just a routine check-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. I’ll see you or Dr. ___ soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’ll get your ERCP biopsy results and follow up. You’re doing well—keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The team will help you with discharge paperwork and getting home safely.
